title: India Just Flew a Field Hospital Halfway Around the World to Help Venezuela Dig Out
excerpt: Operation Amistad sent two C-17s loaded with surgeons, portable ICUs and India's indigenous BHISHM cubes on a 14,300-km airlift — one of New Delhi's longest humanitarian missions ever.
body:
When two earthquakes — magnitude 7.2 and 7.5, separated by seconds — ripped through Venezuela on June 24, they left behind a death toll that has now crossed 1,450, with tens of thousands still unaccounted for. Buildings across La Guaira, just 40 kilometres north of Caracas, folded in on themselves. Entire neighbourhoods vanished.

Two days later, at Hindon Air Force Station outside Delhi, a pair of Indian Air Force C-17 Globemaster III aircraft rolled onto the runway and began one of the longest humanitarian airlifts in Indian military history: Operation Amistad — Spanish for *friendship*.

What India Sent

The two aircraft were carrying an Indian Army Field Hospital Unit drawn from the 60 Para Field Hospital — 41 personnel including nine medical officers trained in disaster-response trauma care. The team was equipped to perform life-saving surgeries, run an intensive-care ward, and manage emergency triage at scale.

The consignment included more than 35 tonnes of humanitarian relief supplies, medicines and medical equipment provided by the Ministry of External Affairs. Among the most significant items: two BHISHM Cubes, India's indigenous portable field hospitals developed under the Aarogya Maitri Project.

Each BHISHM Cube — *Bharat Health Initiative for Sahyog, Hita and Maitri* — consists of 72 portable modules that can be assembled into a fully functional hospital in under 12 minutes. It can treat up to 200 patients and comes equipped with portable ventilators, ultrasound and X-ray machines, defibrillators, a modular operation theatre, a mini-ICU, and independent power and oxygen supplies.

"Operation Amistad underway! Two C-17s took off today for Venezuela with urgent assistance," External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar wrote on X. "India is committed to support the Government and people of Venezuela in this difficult time."

The Logistics Challenge

The C-17 Globemaster has an operational range of roughly 4,400 km — far short of the 14,300 km to Venezuela. Since India does not operate aerial refuelling tankers compatible with this type of mission, the aircraft made planned refuelling stops at friendly nations en route. The scale of the logistics underscored both the ambition and the complexity of projecting humanitarian assistance across hemispheres.

The deployment puts India among more than 20 nations that have sent rescue teams and aid. El Salvador dispatched 300 rescue workers. Mexico sent 250 military rescue personnel and sniffer dogs. Spain flew in a 57-soldier search-and-rescue unit. Switzerland deployed 80 rescuers and 18 metric tonnes of supplies. The United States committed $150 million in aid, two warships, transport aircraft and helicopters.

A Growing Pattern

Operation Amistad is the latest in a pattern of long-range Indian humanitarian deployments. The C-17 fleet has previously spearheaded relief missions to earthquake-hit Türkiye, cyclone-struck Mozambique, and multiple neighbours in South Asia. The BHISHM Cube itself was first deployed during the Türkiye earthquake and has since become a centrepiece of India's disaster diplomacy toolkit.

Venezuelan acting President Delcy Rodriguez expressed gratitude to Prime Minister Modi, who had pledged to "extend all possible assistance." The death toll, now the highest from any Latin American earthquake in years, is expected to rise as rescuers — civilian and international — comb through collapsed buildings where the 72-hour survival window has already closed.

For India, the subtext is strategic as much as humanitarian. New Delhi has been systematically building its reputation as a first-responder power — willing and capable of moving personnel, hardware and medical infrastructure to the other side of the planet at short notice. The diaspora, scattered across 180 countries, watches each deployment as a signal of the country they left behind growing into a role few predicted a generation ago.
